Series::ediff1d¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::ediff1d() const

Consecutive Differences In Logical Flattened Order¶

ediff1d() flattens the receiver in logical row-major order and subtracts each value from its successor:

out[i] = flat[i + 1] - flat[i]

For N input elements, the result is always a one-dimensional series of length max(N - 1, 0). This makes the method a concise choice for gaps in a single logical sequence, including a higher-rank value that should deliberately be treated as one sequence. The difference that crosses a row or plane boundary is included.

Use diff() instead when an axis has semantic meaning and each row, column, or batch member must remain independent. ediff1d() has no axis, order, prepend, or append option; flattening is its defining contract.

Subtraction follows the receiver’s value domain. Integer input produces integer differences, floating input preserves floating precision, and complex input preserves both real and imaginary components. The operation allocates a new, contiguous result on the receiver’s platform. A singleton or empty receiver produces shape [0] rather than throwing.

Reverse Mode¶

For incoming sensitivity g, the flattened source sensitivity is

dx[0]     = -g[0]
dx[i]     =  g[i - 1] - g[i]    for interior positions
dx[N - 1] =  g[N - 2]

The sensitivity is then restored to the receiver’s original shape. Summing all differences telescopes to last - first, while weighted differences expose the full adjacent contribution pattern.

Examples¶

Example 1. Consecutive integer gaps retain integer dtype.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({3, 8, 6, 10}).ediff1d());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[5, -2, 4]

Example 2. Matrix rows are not independent: 16 - 9 is the middle result.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({{1, 4, 9}, {16, 25, 36}}).ediff1d());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[3, 5, 7, 9, 11]

Example 3. Complex subtraction retains both components.

using Complex = std::complex<double>;
pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series(
        std::vector<Complex>{{1.0, 1.0}, {4.0, -1.0}, {2.0, 3.0}}, {3})
        .ediff1d());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=complex128, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[(3.0000-2.0000j), (-2.0000+4.0000j)]

Example 4. A singleton has no adjacent pair.

auto gaps = pluss::make_series({7.0}).ediff1d();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, gaps);
std::cout << "dtype=" << gaps.scalar_type()
          << " dim=" << gaps.dim() << " shape=[" << gaps.size(0) << ']';

Output¶

Series(shape=[0], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=0, contiguous=true)
[]
dtype=float64 dim=1 shape=[0]

Example 5. Weighted differences show how neighbouring terms accumulate during reverse mode.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 5.0, 11.0, 20.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.ediff1d().mul(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 4.0})).sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0000, -1.0000, -2.0000, 4.0000]

See Also¶

  • diff() computes differences along a chosen axis and supports higher orders.

  • cumsum() forms prefix sums rather than adjacent gaps.

  • flatten() makes the sequence interpretation explicit before other operations.
